code.title: Prototype chain lookup and shadowing

followUps:
null ends every chain. Most chains reach Object.prototype first, and its own [[Prototype]] is null, so the lookup stops there and returns undefined for a missing name.

Example: [1,2].foo checks the array, then Array.prototype, then Object.prototype, then null: three hops, no match. Objects made with Object.create(null) have a chain of length zero.

for...in walks the chain on purpose, and Object.keys only looks at the object itself.

for...in lists every enumerable string key of the object and of each prototype. With const d = Object.create({eats:1}); d.name='x', for...in gives name, eats while Object.keys(d) gives only ['name']. Built-in methods are non-enumerable, so they stay hidden. To filter, check Object.hasOwn(d, k) inside the loop.

Engines remember where a property was found, so repeated reads skip the walk.

Objects built the same way share a hidden class (shape) that records property offsets. Each access site keeps an inline cache: for shape S the value is at offset k, or on prototype P. A validity check on the prototypes says the cache is still true. A hit costs about one shape comparison and one memory load. Changing a prototype later invalidates those caches and slows the code down.

code.title: prototype, __proto__ and constructor

followUps:
Arrow functions are not meant to be constructors, so the language gives them no prototype and no [[Construct]] behaviour.

They exist for short callbacks with a lexical this. new (() => 1) throws a TypeError, and (() => 1).prototype is undefined. Methods in classes and object literals (the shorthand form) are also not constructors and have no prototype. This saves memory, because a prototype object is not allocated for every function.

Instances created before the overwrite stay linked to the old prototype, and the new prototype loses its constructor link.

function Car() {}
const a = new Car();
Car.prototype = { drive() {} };
const b = new Car();
a.drive;            // undefined (old link)
b.constructor === Car; // false, it is Object

Fix it with constructor: Car in the literal (or defineProperty to keep it non-enumerable). a instanceof Car also turns false.

It says that Function is itself a function, and every function inherits from Function.prototype, including Function.

So Function.__proto__ and Function.prototype are the same object. Function.prototype is also callable (it is a function that does nothing). The chain ends: Function.prototype.__proto__ === Object.prototype, and Object.prototype.__proto__ === null. It is a bootstrap knot that the engine creates by hand, because functions and objects need each other.

code.title: Implementing the new operator

followUps:
Because the engine checks the result: only an object (or function) can replace the new object, and the new object is the sensible default for anything else.

function P() { this.a = 1; return 42; } then new P() gives {a:1}. A primitive such as 42 cannot carry the instance data, so ignoring it keeps new always yielding an object. Returning {} instead throws away the real instance, which is rare and usually a bug. In derived classes, returning a primitive throws a TypeError.

new.target is the constructor that new was applied to, or undefined in a plain call. It lets a function detect misuse and lets base classes know the real subclass.

In a polyfill you would pass it as an extra hidden argument. For ES5 functions, this instanceof F inside F is the old approximation:

function F() {
  if (!new.target) throw new TypeError('use new');
}

The approximation fails for subclasses and for F.call(Object.create(F.prototype)).

Reflect.construct(Base, args, Derived) runs Base's code but creates the object with Derived.prototype, because the third argument becomes new.target.

function A() { this.n = new.target.name; }
function B() {}
const o = Reflect.construct(A, [], B);
o.n;                  // 'B'
o instanceof B;       // true

That is how class constructors allocate for subclasses, and the only way to call a class constructor on behalf of another class. myNew cannot copy this for built-ins or classes.

code.title: Classes versus ES5 functions

followUps:
ES5 constructors could not create a true Array, because the exotic array object (special length behaviour, internal slots) is allocated only by the built-in constructor.

The old trick Sub.prototype = Object.create(Array.prototype) gives array methods, but length does not update on sub[5] = 1, and Array.isArray(sub) is false. Calling Array.call(this) returns a new array and ignores this. ES6 fixes it because the base constructor allocates the object with new.target.prototype.

Babel used a WeakMap per private field, keyed by the instance, with helpers that throw if the key is missing.

var _x = new WeakMap();
class A { constructor() { _x.set(this, 1); } }
// this.#x  becomes  _classPrivateFieldGet(this, _x)

The map is hidden in module scope, so outside code cannot reach it. It gives real privacy and the same brand-check error, but costs an extra lookup per access. Modern engines now implement #x natively.

Nothing, because TypeScript's private is erased at compile time: it becomes an ordinary public property.

class A { private x = 1; }
// emitted: class A { x = 1; }

So Object.keys, JSON.stringify and a['x'] (with a cast) all see it. It protects only against mistakes during type checking. Use #x when you need runtime privacy.

code.title: extends, super and HomeObject

followUps:
Because the base class constructor allocates this, and until super() returns there is no object yet.

In a derived class, this is uninitialised, so reading it throws a ReferenceError. Only after super(...) returns is this bound and the derived fields set up. Example: constructor(){ this.x = 1; super(); } throws on the first line. Code that does not touch this (for example computing arguments) may run before super().

Yes. class N extends null {} is legal: N.prototype has no prototype, so instances do not inherit from Object.prototype.

But new N() throws a TypeError, because there is no parent constructor for the implicit super(), so this is never created. You can still use it with an explicit constructor that returns Object.create(N.prototype). It is a niche way to make a null-prototype class.

The right side of extends can be any expression that evaluates to a constructor (or null), not just a class name.

const Mixin = B => class extends B {};
class User extends Mixin(Base) {}
class X extends (cond ? A : B) {}

The value must be a constructor with a prototype that is an object or null; anything else throws a TypeError. This is what makes class-factory mixins possible.

code.title: ES5 inheritance: right and wrong

followUps:
Babel's _inherits does the same steps as the correct version, plus some safety checks.

function _inherits(sub, sup) {
  sub.prototype = Object.create(sup.prototype, {
    constructor: { value: sub, writable: true, configurable: true }
  });
  Object.setPrototypeOf(sub, sup);
}

It also throws if sup is neither a function nor null. The child constructor then calls the parent via _super.call(this, ...) (or Reflect.construct for built-ins).

Call it through the parent's prototype with call so this stays the current instance.

Dog.prototype.speak = function () {
  return Animal.prototype.speak.call(this) + ' woof';
};

If Animal.prototype.speak returns 'Rex makes a sound', the result is 'Rex makes a sound woof'. Forgetting .call(this) would run the method with the wrong this.

Object.create(Animal.prototype) links the chains without running the Animal constructor, which is what you want at class-definition time.

new Animal() runs the constructor with no arguments, so this.name = undefined lands on the shared prototype, and any side effects (counters, registering, throwing on missing arguments) fire once for nothing. Instance data should be set per instance with Animal.call(this, name).

code.title: Object.create and null-prototype dictionaries

followUps:
The old trick used a temporary empty constructor so new does the linking.

function create(proto) {
  function F() {}
  F.prototype = proto;
  return new F();
}
const o = create({ hi: 1 });
o.hi;  // 1

The new object has F.prototype as its [[Prototype]], which is proto. It cannot create null-prototype objects and has no descriptor argument.

The method is inherited from Object.prototype, and a null-prototype object has no such link, so the name is undefined and calling it throws a TypeError.

const d = Object.create(null);
d.hasOwnProperty('x');       // TypeError
Object.hasOwn(d, 'x');       // false

Alternatives: Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call(d, 'x') (older) or 'x' in d, which is safe here because nothing is inherited.

Use Object.create(null) or a Map for untrusted keys, and an own-property check for everything else.

One caution: Object.create(null) objects have no hasOwnProperty, so dict.hasOwnProperty(k) throws a TypeError; call Object.hasOwn(dict, k). A Map avoids the key problem entirely, keeps insertion order for any key type, and has a size. The trade-off: no JSON support and slightly different syntax.

code.title: Four kinds of private

followUps:
Because the proxy is a different object from the target, and a private field exists only on the original object.

class A { #x = 1; get x() { return this.#x; } }
const p = new Proxy(new A(), {});
p.x;   // TypeError: this is the proxy

The getter runs with this = p, which has no #x slot. Fix by binding methods to the target in the get trap: typeof v === 'function' ? v.bind(target) : v.

#x in obj returns a boolean without throwing, so it is a cheap exact test for "was this object built by my class".

class A {
  #x;
  static is(o) { return #x in o; }
}
A.is(new A()); // true
A.is({});      // false

With try/catch you would read o.#x and catch the TypeError, which also hides unrelated errors and is slower. It works for any object, including objects with a different prototype.

Use a symbol or a protected-by-convention API, because JavaScript has no real protected.

Options: a naming convention (_x), a module-private Symbol that only the base and subclass files import, a protected method on the base that is not exported on the public type, or a shared WeakMap exported only to subclass modules. The first is easy but public, the others hide the key from callers while subclasses in the same package can still reach it. A #x field cannot be read by a subclass.

code.title: Static members, blocks and inheritance

followUps:
The class binding is visible inside the class body, but only static fields that are already initialised can be read, because initialisers run in source order while the class is being defined.

Inside a static initialiser this and the class name both refer to the class, so static a = 1; static b = Foo.a + 1; gives b = 2. Reading a static declared further down gives undefined. The binding is not usable in the extends expression itself (class Foo extends Foo.x throws a ReferenceError).

Use a plain module-level function when the code does not need class state, and a static method when it belongs to the class and needs inheritance or private statics.

Module functions are simpler, tree-shake well and are easy to mock. Static methods can be overridden in subclasses, use this for polymorphic factories (new this()), and reach private statics. Example: Money.fromCents(5) reads well as a factory, while formatDate(d) that touches no class should be a function.

Keep the single instance in a private static field and create it on first use.

class Config {
  static #inst = null;
  static get() { return Config.#inst ??= new Config(); }
  constructor() { if (Config.#inst) throw new Error('use get()'); }
}

Two calls to Config.get() return the same object. Note that modules are cached too, so exporting one instance (export const config = new Config()) is often the simpler singleton.

code.title: How instanceof works and fails

followUps:
The same walk as instanceof: start at Object.getPrototypeOf(x) and compare each link to C.prototype by identity.

function inst(x, C) {
  if (x === null || typeof x !== 'object' && typeof x !== 'function') return false;
  for (let p = Object.getPrototypeOf(x); p !== null; p = Object.getPrototypeOf(p))
    if (p === C.prototype) return true;
  return false;
}

Time is O(chain length), space O(1). It ignores Symbol.hasInstance, which the real operator checks first.

Because each copy of the library defines its own class object, and instanceof compares prototypes by identity.

If package A loads lib@1 and package B loads lib@2 (or the same version installed twice), an error created by one has the prototype of that copy, so err instanceof LibError in the other is false. Fix by deduplicating the dependency, declaring it a peer dependency, or checking a tag such as err.name === 'LibError', a Symbol.for brand or a type guard.

isPrototypeOf works on objects, not constructors: A.prototype.isPrototypeOf(x) asks whether A.prototype is somewhere on x's chain.

It does not consult Symbol.hasInstance and does not need a function on the right. So it works with an Object.create(proto) base that has no constructor: base.isPrototypeOf(child). Both walk the same chain and use identity, so they share the cross-realm and replaced-prototype problems.

code.title: Overridable call in a constructor

followUps:
They behave almost the same: all of them call the override, but they differ in what the child's fields hold at that moment.

Java: the child's fields exist with default values (0, null) and its initialisers run after super(), so the override reads null. C#: the child's field initialisers run before the base constructor, so they are already set (the opposite of Java and JavaScript). C++: during a base constructor the object is still the base type, so virtual calls go to the base version. JavaScript: fields are undefined (or a TypeError for #private).

It decides whether class fields are created with defineProperty (new standard) or with plain assignment (old TypeScript behaviour).

With useDefineForClassFields: true (default for targets ES2022 and later), class A { x?: number } emits x;, which creates an own property set to undefined. This can overwrite a value set by the base constructor. With false, a field without an initialiser emits nothing, and one with an initialiser becomes this.x = ... in the constructor, which can trigger setters.

Component frameworks use it, because they must create the object first and attach it to a host before running user code.

Web Components use connectedCallback, which the browser calls only after the element is in the DOM. React class components have componentDidMount, Angular has ngOnInit. The reasons are to avoid virtual calls on half-built objects and to run setup that needs the environment (DOM, injected services). Factory functions such as static create() give the same effect in plain code.

code.title: Prototype pollution and a safe merge

followUps:
Because JSON.parse only creates an own property named "__proto__"; it does not change the object's prototype.

JSON.parse('{"__proto__":{"x":1}}') gives an object whose Object.keys is ['__proto__'] and ({}).x stays undefined. Harm starts when later code copies that key with target[key] = ... or a recursive merge, because assignment goes through the inherited __proto__ setter and reaches Object.prototype.

Skip the three dangerous keys, only recurse into own properties, and write into fresh objects.

function merge(t, s) {
  for (const k of Object.keys(s)) {
    if (k === '__proto__' || k === 'constructor' || k === 'prototype') continue;
    if (s[k] && typeof s[k] === 'object') { if (!Object.hasOwn(t, k)) t[k] = {}; merge(t[k], s[k]); }
    else t[k] = s[k];
  }
  return t;
}

It costs O(total keys). Creating t with Object.create(null) adds another layer of defence.

A gadget is existing code that reads a property that the attacker can now supply through the polluted prototype.

Example: a template engine calls opts.sourceURL or builds a function from opts.compileDebug; if the options object does not define it, the lookup reaches Object.prototype and finds the attacker's string, which gets compiled and run. Similar tricks work with child_process options such as shell or env. Defence: use own-property checks, null-prototype option objects, and schema validation.

code.title: Mixins versus composition

followUps:
React replaced mixins with hooks because mixins shared one namespace and one lifecycle, which made components hard to follow.

Two mixins could define the same method name or state key, and both ran on every lifecycle call, so nobody could tell where a value came from. A hook such as useWindowSize() is just a function that owns its state and returns it, so names are chosen by the caller and dependencies are explicit. It is composition by function call instead of by merging into one object.

Type a mixin as a function from a constructor type to a class that adds members.

type Ctor<T = {}> = new (...args: any[]) => T;
function Eventful<B extends Ctor>(Base: B) {
  return class extends Base { on(n: string) {} };
}
class User extends Eventful(Model) {}

The result type is an intersection of the base instance type and the added members. Limits: private or protected members in an exported mixin class are not allowed, and the constructor must take ...args: any[].

A hierarchy turns into a smell when you cannot explain a class without opening three parents, or subclasses override most parent methods.

Warning signs: more than about three levels, a child that ignores or disables parent behaviour (breaking the is-a rule), flags like isSpecial in the base class, and tests that need the whole chain to be built. Example: Square extends Rectangle that overrides both setters. Refactor by giving the parent role to a field (composition) and sharing code through small functions.

code.title: Stable object shapes

followUps:
The three names say how many object shapes (hidden classes) an access site has seen: one, a few, or many.

Monomorphic: one shape, so the cache is one compare and one load. Polymorphic: 2 to 4 shapes (V8 allows up to 4), checked one after another. Megamorphic: more than that, so V8 drops to a slower shared hash lookup. Example: f(o) called with 2 object shapes is polymorphic; with 10 different shapes it is megamorphic and several times slower.

Because class fields are created in the same order every time, all instances get the same hidden class.

class P { x = 0; y = 0; constructor(a) { this.x = a; } }

Every new P() adds x then y, so access sites stay monomorphic. Setting properties conditionally or in different orders creates branching shapes ({a,b} vs {b,a}). Declaring all fields up front also avoids later shape transitions that waste memory.

Measure with a benchmark that runs the hot code many times on realistic data, then ask the engine what it did using --trace-ic and --trace-deopt.

Steps: (1) warm up, then time the loop with stable versus mixed shapes (for example 200000 objects, 20 repeats); (2) run node --trace-deopt app.js to list deoptimisations; (3) run with --allow-natives-syntax and call %HasFastProperties(o) to see whether an object fell into dictionary mode; (4) use the Chrome DevTools profiler. Compare timings, not guesses.
